e: note:'US Gulf Coast LNG terminals (Sabine Pass, Freeport, Corpus Christi, Calcasieu Pass) have become the dominant UK LNG source. Trinidad Atlantic LNG and smaller volumes from other Americas origins are included here. All cargoes cross the North Atlantic directly to South Hook (Milford Haven) or Isle of Grain (Kent). No maritime chokepoint on any of these routes. The US LNG build-out, enabled by the shale revolution, is the single largest structural shift in UK gas supply security since North Sea production peak.'

e: note:'Norway (Hammerfest LNG, Snohvit field on the Barents Sea coast) ships via the Norwegian Sea directly to UK terminals. No chokepoint. Russia (Yamal LNG, Sabetta terminal on the Yamal Peninsula) routes westbound via the Northern Sea Route and Norwegian Sea to Isle of Grain. Russian LNG was not covered by the UK commodity ban that applied to crude oil; imports have continued under existing contracts while the government presses for phase-down. Combined these two North Sea-corridor sources represent 18% of UK LNG with no strategic maritime chokepoint on either supply path.'

e: note:'Algerian LNG from the Skikda and Arzew liquefaction plants on the Mediterranean coast transits via Gibraltar into the Atlantic to reach UK terminals. No strategic maritime chokepoint. Algeria merges with Qatari cargoes at Gibraltar, representing the full Mediterranean LNG approach to the UK. Algeria has supplied European gas markets since the 1970s and remains a consistent mid-tier supplier despite constraints from rising domestic consumption.'

e: note:'Qatar underpins UK long-term LNG contracts, primarily via the South Hook terminal in Milford Haven (capacity 21 bcm/yr, 60% owned by QatarEnergy). Cargoes load at Ras Laffan on the Persian Gulf coast and must clear Hormuz, then Bab el-Mandeb, then the Suez Canal, before emerging into the Mediterranean and clearing Gibraltar to reach South Hook. Four successive chokepoints. A Hormuz closure stops Qatar supply entirely; there is no alternative Qatari export terminal outside the Persian Gulf.'

e: note:'The Strait of Hormuz is the mandatory exit for all LNG loaded at Ras Laffan inside the Persian Gulf. At 27% of UK LNG, Qatar\'s entire contracted supply transits Hormuz. Compare this with UK crude, where only 8% transits Hormuz. LNG vessels (Q-Flex and Q-Max class) cannot be rerouted to alternative loading points; Ras Laffan is Qatar\'s only export terminal. After Hormuz, Qatar LNG continues to Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal before reaching the Mediterranean.'

e: note:'Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal are a sequential double chokepoint for Qatari LNG bound for the UK. After transiting Hormuz, LNG carriers cross the Arabian Sea, clear Bab el-Mandeb into the Red Sea, then transit the Suez Canal before emerging into the Mediterranean. Either node can independently block the route: Bab through military interdiction, Suez through political closure or accident. Since late 2023, Houthi attacks have made Bab el-Mandeb the most actively contested maritime chokepoint globally. Most LNG operators have diverted around the Cape of Good Hope, adding 10 to 12 days of voyage time and substantially increasing delivered gas costs to the UK.'

e: note:'The Strait of Gibraltar is the final chokepoint for Mediterranean-routed LNG before it enters the Atlantic for the UK. Qatar cargoes (27%), after clearing Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb, and the Suez Canal, emerge into the Mediterranean and transit Gibraltar. Algerian LNG (8%) loads directly into the Mediterranean and joins at Gibraltar. Together they represent 35% of UK LNG, all converging at this single Atlantic entry point. Gibraltar itself is not considered a strategic chokepoint (14km width, no single-nation control), but it is the geographic confluence of the most supply-chain-complex LNG routes serving the UK market.'

e: note:'UK LNG imports averaged approximately 14 to 16 billion cubic metres per year in 2024. Primary receiving terminals: South Hook LNG (Milford Haven, Wales, primarily Qatari), Dragon LNG (also Milford Haven), and Isle of Grain LNG (Kent, primarily US and Russian). The UK grid connects these terminals to the National Transmission System for distribution.'
